title: Shraddha Kapoor Disappears Into Maharashtra's Greatest Folk Legend. Eetha Is Her Biggest Swing Yet.
excerpt: She shot a five-day song sequence with 800 performers. She learned Lavani from scratch. And on August 28, she becomes Vithabai Narayangaonkar — the woman who won two President's Awards and still died forgotten.
body:
The first thing you notice in the leaked set photos from Bhor, Maharashtra, is the scale. Shraddha Kapoor stands at the centre of a crowd — 800 background performers, all in period costume, recreating one of the most emotionally charged Tamasha performances in Marathi folk history. It's the final song sequence of Eetha, and it reportedly took five days to shoot. When the cameras stopped rolling, it marked the end of a principal photography schedule that had stretched from November 2025 through early 2026, across multiple locations in Maharashtra. The film now has a date: August 28, 2026 — a Raksha Bandhan release that pits it directly against Sidharth Malhotra and Tamannaah Bhatia's Vvan.

This is not Stree. This is not even close.

The Woman Behind the Legend

Eetha is based on the life of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar, one of Maharashtra's most revered Tamasha and Lavani performers. Born in Pandharpur, Solapur district, in July 1935, Vithabai came from a family steeped in traditional folk performance. She started young, and by her twenties, she was the most magnetic presence on the Tamasha stage — powerful voice, explosive energy, a performer who could command a crowd of thousands in an open-air amphitheatre with nothing but her body and her voice.

She received two President's Awards — in 1957 and 1990 — for her contributions to Indian folk culture. But behind the awards and the adulation was a life shaped by caste prejudice, personal hardship, and the relentless economics of a dying art form. Vithabai's story is not just a celebration; it's a reckoning with what India asks of its artists, especially those born outside the mainstream.

Director Laxman Utekar, who last delivered the blockbuster Chhaava (2025) with Vicky Kaushal, has reportedly crafted the film as a sweeping tribute to Maharashtra's Lavani tradition. The narrative stretches from the 1940s to the 1990s — five decades of a woman fighting to be seen, heard, and remembered.

Shraddha's Biggest Swing Yet

Let's be honest: Shraddha Kapoor's filmography has been commercially brilliant but performance-light. Stree and Stree 2 were massive, genre-defining hits, but they never really asked her to carry dramatic weight. Eetha does. This is her Gangubai, her Mary Kom — an author-backed biographical role that requires physical transformation, dialect work, and the kind of emotional range she hasn't been asked to deliver before.

Reports suggest she underwent extensive preparation to authentically inhabit Vithabai's world — learning Lavani movement, working with Marathi folk performers, and immersing herself in the cultural landscape of rural Maharashtra. For an actress who built her stardom on urban rom-coms and horror-comedies, this is the boldest creative bet of her career.

The supporting cast adds serious weight. Randeep Hooda, one of Hindi cinema's most consistently underrated actors, takes a pivotal role, alongside Mohammed Zeeshan Ayyub, who has quietly become one of Bollywood's most reliable scene-stealers.

The Maddock Machine

Dinesh Vijan's Maddock Films is having a year. The studio that built the Stree horror-comedy universe and launched Chhaava to blockbuster status is now doubling down on biographical dramas — Eetha on August 28 and Prahaar – The Ujjwal Nikam Story, starring Rajkummar Rao, on August 7. Two films from the same banner in the same month is rare. Two films from the same banner in the same month, both based on real-life icons from Maharashtra, is unprecedented.

Music for Eetha has been composed by Ajay-Atul, the powerhouse duo behind the Singham franchise and Deva Shree Ganesha. If anyone can translate Lavani into a mainstream Bollywood soundscape without losing its soul, it's them.

Why Diaspora Audiences Should Care

Vithabai Narayangaonkar's name may not be instantly recognisable to NRI audiences, but her story carries universal weight — an artist from a marginalised community who redefined an entire art form, won national recognition, and still died without the institutional support she deserved. For the Marathi diaspora, this is a cultural landmark. For everyone else, it's a window into a performance tradition that most Hindi-language cinema has never bothered to explore.

Eetha arrives in theatres worldwide on August 28, 2026. Mark it.
